topics.title: Trigonometric Ratios
topics.concept:
What are Trigonometric Ratios?

Trigonometric Ratios are the mathematical relationships that connect the acute angles of a right-angled triangle to the lengths of its sides. The word trigonometry comes from Greek words meaning "triangle measurement." These ratios allow us to calculate unknown distances or angles simply by using fractions formed by the sides of a triangle.

In a right-angled triangle, we name the three sides based on their position relative to a chosen target angle, which we usually call theta (written as a symbol or spelled out). The three sides are:

  • Hypotenuse: The absolute longest side, always located directly across from the 90-degree right angle.
  • Perpendicular (or Opposite): The side that stands directly facing opposite our chosen angle theta.
  • Base (or Adjacent): The side that lies next to our angle theta, running between theta and the right angle.

Imagine you are looking up at the top of a giant smartphone screen resting on a table. The straight height of the screen from the table is the perpendicular, the flat distance along the table from your eyes to the screen base is the base, and your straight line of sight up to the top corner is the hypotenuse.

There are exactly six distinct trigonometric ratios. Three are primary ratios, and three are reciprocal ratios (meaning they are flipped upside down):

Ratio NameAbbreviationFractional DefinitionReciprocal Relationship
**Cosine**cosBase / Hypotenuse1 / sec
**Tangent**tanPerpendicular / Base1 / cot
**Cosecant**cscHypotenuse / Perpendicular1 / sin
**Secant**secHypotenuse / Base1 / cos
**Cotangent**cotBase / Perpendicular1 / tan

sections.content:
What are Trigonometric Ratios?

Trigonometric Ratios are the mathematical relationships that connect the acute angles of a right-angled triangle to the lengths of its sides. The word trigonometry comes from Greek words meaning "triangle measurement." These ratios allow us to calculate unknown distances or angles simply by using fractions formed by the sides of a triangle.

In a right-angled triangle, we name the three sides based on their position relative to a chosen target angle, which we usually call theta (written as a symbol or spelled out). The three sides are:

Hypotenuse: The absolute longest side, always located directly across from the 90-degree right angle. Perpendicular (or Opposite): The side that stands directly facing opposite our chosen angle theta. * Base (or Adjacent): The side that lies next to our angle theta, running between theta and the right angle.

Imagine you are looking up at the top of a giant smartphone screen resting on a table. The straight height of the screen from the table is the perpendicular, the flat distance along the table from your eyes to the screen base is the base, and your straight line of sight up to the top corner is the hypotenuse.

There are exactly six distinct trigonometric ratios. Three are primary ratios, and three are reciprocal ratios (meaning they are flipped upside down):

Ratio NameAbbreviationFractional DefinitionReciprocal Relationship
------------
SinesinPerpendicular / Hypotenuse1 / csc
CosinecosBase / Hypotenuse1 / sec
TangenttanPerpendicular / Base1 / cot
CosecantcscHypotenuse / Perpendicular1 / sin
SecantsecHypotenuse / Base1 / cos
CotangentcotBase / Perpendicular1 / tan

DIAGRAM 1: SIDE LABELS RELATIVE TO THE CHOSEN ANGLE THETA

                  A
                  |\
                  | \
                  |  \  Hypotenuse
Perpendicular     |   \
(Opposite to      |    \
 Angle Theta)     |     \
                  |______\
                  C  Base B (Angle Theta is here)
             (Right Angle)


DIAGRAM 2: THE PRIMARY VS RECIPROCAL MATCHING FLOW

    PRIMARY RATIOS                      RECIPROCAL RATIOS
  +----------------+                 +---------------------+
  | sin = Perp/Hyp | <=============> | csc = Hyp/Perp      |
  | cos = Base/Hyp | <=============> | sec = Hyp/Base      |
  | tan = Perp/Base| <=============> | cot = Base/Perp     |
  +----------------+                 +---------------------+

points: Trigonometric ratios are only valid inside **right-angled triangles**.
The **perpendicular** side is not always vertical; it is always whichever side is directly across from the chosen angle.
**Sine**, **Cosine**, and **Tangent** are the core ratios.
**Cosecant**, **Secant**, and **Cotangent** are formed by flipping the core ratios upside down.
SOH-CAH-TOA is a quick mnemonic memory trick: **S**ine is **O**pposite/**H**ypotenuse, **C**osine is **A**djacent/**H**ypotenuse, and **T**angent is **O**pposite/**A**djacent.

topics.title: Ratios of Standard Angles
topics.concept:
What are Ratios of Standard Angles?

The Ratios of Standard Angles are fixed, unchanging numerical values for the trigonometric ratios of specific geometric angles that appear frequently in engineering and science. These standard angles are 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 degrees.

Instead of measuring sides with a ruler every time you see a 30-degree angle, mathematicians have proved that a 30-degree right triangle always has a perpendicular that is exactly half the length of its hypotenuse. This means that the sine of 30 degrees will always equal 1/2, no matter how small or large the actual physical triangle is.

These values are derived directly from two special geometric setups:

  1. An isosceles right triangle (which contains two 45-degree angles).
  2. An equilateral triangle chopped exactly in half down its center height line (which creates 30-degree and 60-degree angles).

Here is the complete standard reference value grid:

Angle (degrees)sincostancscseccot
**30°**1/2(√3)/21/√322/√3√3
**45°**1/√21/√21√2√21
**60°**(√3)/21/2√32/√321/√3
**90°**10Not Defined1Not Defined0

sections.content:
What are Ratios of Standard Angles?

The Ratios of Standard Angles are fixed, unchanging numerical values for the trigonometric ratios of specific geometric angles that appear frequently in engineering and science. These standard angles are 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 degrees.

Instead of measuring sides with a ruler every time you see a 30-degree angle, mathematicians have proved that a 30-degree right triangle always has a perpendicular that is exactly half the length of its hypotenuse. This means that the sine of 30 degrees will always equal 1/2, no matter how small or large the actual physical triangle is.

These values are derived directly from two special geometric setups:

1. An isosceles right triangle (which contains two 45-degree angles). 2. An equilateral triangle chopped exactly in half down its center height line (which creates 30-degree and 60-degree angles).

Here is the complete standard reference value grid:

Angle (degrees)sincostancscseccot
---------------------
0°010Not Defined1Not Defined
30°1/2(√3)/21/√322/√3√3
45°1/√21/√21√2√21
60°(√3)/21/2√32/√321/√3
90°10Not Defined1Not Defined0

DIAGRAM 1: THE 45-45-90 SPECIAL RIGHT TRIANGLE REFERENCE
                 
                 /\
                /  \
            √2 /    \ 1
              /      \
             /________\
             45°   1   90°
             
  - sin 45° = 1/√2
  - cos 45° = 1/√2
  - tan 45° = 1


DIAGRAM 2: THE 30-60-90 HALF-EQUILATERAL TRIANGLE REFERENCE

                 /\ 30°
                /  |
               /   |
             2/    | √3
             /     |
            /______|
          60°   1  90°

  - sin 30° = 1/2  ,  sin 60° = √3/2
  - cos 30° = √3/2 ,  cos 60° = 1/2

points: The values of **sin** increase from 0 to 1 as the angle goes from 0° to 90°.
The values of **cos** decrease from 1 to 0 as the angle goes from 0° to 90°.
**tan 90°** and **csc 0°** are mathematically **not defined** because their definitions require dividing by zero.
The square of a ratio like sin² 45° simply means you find sin 45° first, and then multiply that number by itself.
Remembering the two special reference triangles allows you to reconstruct the entire standard table from memory.

topics.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Complementary Angles
topics.concept:
What are Complementary Angle Relationships in Trigonometry?

Complementary Angles are any two angles that add up to a clean total of exactly 90 degrees. In any right-angled triangle, since the right angle uses up 90 degrees of the internal 180-degree total, the remaining two acute angles must always be complementary to each other. If one angle is theta, the other angle is automatically (90° - theta).

Because these two angles share the same right triangle, the perpendicular side for one angle automatically becomes the base side for the other angle. This creates an interesting swap-over effect where the sine value of one angle matches the cosine value of its complement.

Think of it like a reflection. The prefix "co-" in cosine, cotangent, and cosecant literally stands for "complementary." So, Cosine means the "Sine of the Complement."

The complete set of complementary angle transformation equations is shown below:

Starting Ratio FormComplementary Equivalent Form
**cos (90° - theta)**sin theta
**tan (90° - theta)**cot theta
**cot (90° - theta)**tan theta
**sec (90° - theta)**csc theta
**csc (90° - theta)**sec theta

sections.content:
What are Complementary Angle Relationships in Trigonometry?

Complementary Angles are any two angles that add up to a clean total of exactly 90 degrees. In any right-angled triangle, since the right angle uses up 90 degrees of the internal 180-degree total, the remaining two acute angles must always be complementary to each other. If one angle is theta, the other angle is automatically (90° - theta).

Because these two angles share the same right triangle, the perpendicular side for one angle automatically becomes the base side for the other angle. This creates an interesting swap-over effect where the sine value of one angle matches the cosine value of its complement.

Think of it like a reflection. The prefix "co-" in cosine, cotangent, and cosecant literally stands for "complementary." So, Cosine means the "Sine of the Complement."

The complete set of complementary angle transformation equations is shown below:

Starting Ratio FormComplementary Equivalent Form
------
sin (90° - theta)cos theta
cos (90° - theta)sin theta
tan (90° - theta)cot theta
cot (90° - theta)tan theta
sec (90° - theta)csc theta
csc (90° - theta)sec theta

DIAGRAM 1: THE INTERNAL ANGLE BALANCE OF A RIGHT TRIANGLE

                     /\ (90° - Theta)
                    /  \
                   /    \
                  /      \
                 /________\
                Theta      90°
                
  - If you look from the bottom angle, sin(Theta) = Opposite / Hypotenuse
  - If you look from the top angle, cos(90° - Theta) uses the exact same fraction!


DIAGRAM 2: TRANSFORMATION PAIR LINKS

    [ sin ] <=======================> [ cos ]
    [ tan ] <=======================> [ cot ]
    [ sec ] <=======================> [ csc ]

points: Complementary angle adjustments apply when angles sum up to **90°**.
**Sine** shifts over into **Cosine**, and vice-versa.
**Tangent** shifts over into **Cotangent**, and vice-versa.
**Secant** shifts over into **Cosecant**, and vice-versa.
When dealing with non-standard angles (like 18° or 72°) in a fraction, look for complementary pairs that can be converted to match and cancel out.

topics.title: Simple Identities Involving sin, cos, and tan
topics.concept:
What are Trigonometric Identities?

A Trigonometric Identity is an algebraic equation involving trigonometric functions that remains true for every single value substituted into the angle variable. Unlike a regular equation that you solve for a specific x value, an identity is a universal rule of balance.

There are two major sets of simple identities that form the foundation of triangle algebra:

  1. Quotient Identities: These identities show how the tangent ratio is built directly by dividing the sine ratio by the cosine ratio.
  • tan theta = sin theta / cos theta
  • cot theta = cos theta / sin theta
  1. Pythagorean Identities: These identities are derived by combining the Pythagoras Theorem (\(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\)) with our fundamental trigonometric fraction definitions. The most important foundational Pythagorean identity is:
  • sin² theta + cos² theta = 1

Think of this like an algebraic currency exchange. If you are working through a long mathematical expression and you have a mix of sine terms and cosine terms, you can use these identities to trade them out and rewrite everything in a single clean form.

sections.content:
What are Trigonometric Identities?

A Trigonometric Identity is an algebraic equation involving trigonometric functions that remains true for every single value substituted into the angle variable. Unlike a regular equation that you solve for a specific x value, an identity is a universal rule of balance.

There are two major sets of simple identities that form the foundation of triangle algebra:

1. Quotient Identities: These identities show how the tangent ratio is built directly by dividing the sine ratio by the cosine ratio. tan theta = sin theta / cos theta cot theta = cos theta / sin theta

2. Pythagorean Identities: These identities are derived by combining the Pythagoras Theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) with our fundamental trigonometric fraction definitions. The most important foundational Pythagorean identity is: * sin² theta + cos² theta = 1

Think of this like an algebraic currency exchange. If you are working through a long mathematical expression and you have a mix of sine terms and cosine terms, you can use these identities to trade them out and rewrite everything in a single clean form.

DIAGRAM 1: THE FOUNDATIONAL PYTHAGOREAN SQUARE IDENTITY
 
               _________________________________
              |                                 |
              |     sin² Theta + cos² Theta = 1  |
              |_________________________________|
                               |
               +---------------|---------------+
               |                               |
       [ Rearranged Form 1 ]           [ Rearranged Form 2 ]
       sin² Theta = 1 - cos² Theta     cos² Theta = 1 - sin² Theta


DIAGRAM 2: THE QUOTIENT COMPOSITION BLOCK
 
          +---------------+
          |   sin Theta   |
          | ------------- |  ==============>  [ tan Theta ]
          |   cos Theta   |
          +---------------+

points: An identity is a universal rule that stays true for any angle value.
**tan theta** can always be broken down into the fraction **sin theta / cos theta**.
The core Pythagorean relationship states that **sin² theta + cos² theta = 1**.
This square identity can be rearranged into two useful subtraction layouts: **sin² theta = 1 - sin² theta** or **cos² theta = 1 - sin² theta**.
When trying to simplify a complex looking trigonometric expression, a great strategy is to convert every term into sin and cos right at the start.

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle, if the perpendicular is 5 cm and the hypotenuse is 13 cm, what is the value of cos theta?
questions.explanation: Base = √(13² - 5²) = 12 cm. cos theta = Base / Hypotenuse = 12/13.

questions.q: What is the exact numerical value of tan 45° + cos 60°?

questions.explanation: Since 18° + 72° = 90°, sin 18° = cos 72°. The fraction equals 1.

questions.q: Which of the following is equivalent to 1 - cos² theta?
questions.explanation: This is a direct rearrangement of the fundamental identity sin² theta + cos² theta = 1.

questions.q: If sin theta = cos theta for an acute angle theta, what is the measurement of the angle?
questions.explanation: From the standard angle values, both sin 45° and cos 45° equal 1/√2.

questions.q: Evaluate the following product: tan 30° × cot 30°.
questions.explanation: Tangent and cotangent are reciprocals of each other, so their product is always 1.

questions.q: If cos A = 4/5, find the value of tan A.
Simplify the expression completely: cos (90° - theta).
questions.explanation: This is a direct application of the complementary angle transformation rule.

questions.q: What is the value of sin² 30° + cos² 30°?
questions.explanation: According to the Pythagorean identity, sin² theta + cos² theta = 1 for any angle.

questions.q: If tan theta = √3, what is the value of the acute angle theta?
questions.explanation: According to the standard trigonometric ratios table, tan 60° = √3.

questions.q: Evaluate the following continuous product chain: tan 1° × tan 2° × tan 3° × ... × tan 88° × tan 89°.
questions.explanation: Pair terms like tan 1° × tan 89° = tan 1° × cot 1° = 1. tan 45° in the middle is 1. All terms multiply to 1.

questions.q: If sin theta + sin² theta = 1, find the value of the expression (cos² theta + cos⁴ theta).
questions.explanation: From the given info, sin theta = 1 - sin² theta = cos² theta. Substitute this into the target expression: sin theta + sin² theta = 1.

questions.q: An observer looks up at the top of a tower at an angle of 45°. If the observer moves 10 meters further away from the tower base, the angle shifts to 30°. Find the height of the tower.
questions.explanation: Let height be h. Base 1 = h × cot 45° = h. Base 2 = h × cot 30° = h√3. h√3 - h = 10 -> h(√3 - 1) = 10 -> h = 10 / (√3 - 1).

questions.q: Eliminate the angle parameter theta from the pair of parametric equations: x = a × cos theta and y = b × sin theta.
questions.explanation: Rearrange to x/a = cos theta and y/b = sin theta. Square and add them: (x/a)² + (y/b)² = cos² theta + sin² theta = 1.

questions.q: If sec theta + tan theta = p, determine the value of sec theta in terms of the variable p.
questions.explanation: Since sec²x - tan²x = 1, sec x - tan x = 1/p. Add this to the given equation: 2 × sec x = p + 1/p = (p² + 1)/p -> sec x = (p² + 1)/2p.

questions.q: Evaluate the numerical value of the expression: 2 × (sin⁶ theta + cos⁶ theta) - 3 × (sin⁴ theta + cos⁴ theta) + 1.
questions.explanation: Let sin theta = 1 and cos theta = 0 (using angle 90°). Expression becomes: 2 × (1 + 0) - 3 × (1 + 0) + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0. True for all angles.
